posts.title: How to install AppDrop
posts.excerpt: The best store for downloading apps on your jailbroken iOS device.
posts.content:
Welcome to the first blog post on this page.
Today, I’ll show you how to install AppDrop—the best store for those with a jailbroken Apple device.

So, let’s get started.
Open Cydia or Zebra, go to Sources, and tap the "+" icon.
Enter the following source URL: https://adrienrl1.github.io/cydia/

Note: If you are using a much older version of iOS, use http://adrienrl1.github.io/cydia/ instead.

Once that’s done, tap on the "AdrienRL" source, go to "All Packages," and then select "AppDrop."
Tap "Modify" > "Install."

After the installation is complete, the app will appear on your home screen.

OPENING THE APP:
When you open the app, you’ll be greeted by a home screen containing various folders filled with applications.

It uses archive.org to retrieve the .ipa files.

Make sure you have Filza File Manager installed so you can view the downloaded IPA files.

Thanks for reading, and see you in the next post!

posts.title: Rooting Android and Its Consequences: Should I Really Root My Old Device?
posts.excerpt: Thinking about rooting your old Android phone? Explore the benefits, risks, security concerns and everything you should consider before taking control of your device.
posts.content:
# Rooting Android and Its Consequences: Should I Really Root My Old Device?

**Android has always been known for its flexibility.** Unlike many other mobile operating systems, it gives users a considerable amount of control over how their devices look and behave. But there is one subject that has remained part of the Android community for years: rooting.

For some people, rooting is the best way to get more out of an older smartphone. For others, it is an unnecessary risk that can turn a perfectly usable device into a frustrating experience.

So, is rooting still worth it, especially if you have an older Android device sitting around?

Let's take a closer look.

## What exactly is rooting?

Android is built on Linux, and like other Linux-based systems, it uses different permission levels to control what users and applications can access.

Normally, Android users operate without full administrative privileges. This is intentional. It helps protect important system components and prevents applications from making changes that could affect the entire device.

Root access removes many of those restrictions by giving the user administrator-level permissions.

In simple terms, rooting gives you much deeper control over Android. You can access areas of the system that are normally restricted, use certain advanced applications and make modifications that would otherwise be impossible.

However, having more control also means having more responsibility.

## Why do people root their Android devices?

There was a time when rooting was almost a hobby for Android enthusiasts. Online communities were full of people experimenting with custom ROMs, kernels, themes and modifications.

One of the biggest reasons was customization. Users wanted to change things that manufacturers did not allow them to modify, from system behavior to visual elements.

Another reason was software support. Many older smartphones stopped receiving official Android updates long before their hardware became completely unusable. Custom ROMs offered another possibility, allowing some devices to run newer versions of Android through community-developed software.

There were also applications that required root access to perform advanced tasks, such as managing certain system settings or creating complete device backups.

For someone who enjoys experimenting with technology, it is easy to understand the appeal.

## The advantages of rooting an old device

Rooting can make an older Android phone more interesting to use, particularly if you enjoy exploring how the operating system works.

Some of the potential benefits include:

**More control over the system.** Root access allows advanced modifications that are unavailable on a standard Android installation.

**Greater customization.** Certain tools can change system behavior and provide additional options for experienced users.

**Custom ROM compatibility.** Depending on the device and its developer community, alternative Android distributions may offer a different experience or extend software support.

**Access to advanced applications.** Some utilities offer additional functionality when root permissions are available.

Still, these benefits depend heavily on the exact device, its Android version and the quality of the available community support.

Rooting does not magically improve a phone's processor, increase its physical memory or repair an aging battery. It simply gives you more freedom to modify the software.

## The consequences nobody should ignore

This is where things become more complicated.

Rooting is not a harmless customization option. Depending on how it is performed and how the device is configured afterward, it can introduce several problems.

**Security is one of the biggest concerns.**

Android's permission system exists for a reason. When an application receives root access, it may gain the ability to make changes far beyond what an ordinary application can do. Giving those permissions to an untrusted application can put personal information and the entire system at risk.

There is also the possibility of losing access to certain services. Some banking applications, games and streaming platforms check whether a device meets their security requirements. A rooted device may fail those checks, even if everything appears to work normally.

Updates can become another issue. Official system updates may no longer install as expected, particularly when system components have been modified. Some devices also have manufacturer-specific restrictions that complicate the process.

And then there is the possibility of making the device unusable. Incorrect modifications can prevent Android from starting properly. Recovery may be possible, but it is not guaranteed, and some situations require specialized repair.

Warranty coverage is another consideration. The consequences vary by manufacturer and local consumer protection laws, so it is worth checking the applicable terms before making changes.

## Is rooting worth it in 2026?

The answer depends on what you want to achieve.

If you have an old Android phone that you no longer use as your primary device, rooting might be an interesting project. It can be a way to learn more about Android, explore alternative software and understand how mobile operating systems work.

However, if the device is still your everyday phone, the decision deserves much more consideration.

Losing access to banking services, encountering update problems or weakening the device's security can easily outweigh the benefits of having additional customization options.

It is also important to remember that rooting is not the only way to improve an older Android experience. Removing unnecessary applications, freeing up storage, keeping applications updated and using lighter alternatives can already make a difference without changing the system's security model.

## Before making your decision

There are a few things worth considering before modifying an older device:

- Check whether your exact model has reliable community support.
- Understand the security implications of granting root permissions.
- Consider whether you actually need the features that root provides.
- Make sure you understand the recovery options available for your device.
- Think about whether you depend on applications that may reject rooted devices.

Most importantly, do not root a device just because someone online claims it will make Android faster. That is not what root access is designed to do.

## Final thoughts

Rooting remains one of the most interesting parts of Android's history and identity. It represents something that has always attracted enthusiasts to the platform: the ability to experiment, customize and take control of their own devices.

But the Android world has changed. Security requirements have become stricter, applications increasingly rely on device integrity checks, and manufacturers have introduced more restrictions.

For an old smartphone used as a secondary device or a personal technology project, rooting can still be worth exploring. For a phone that contains your everyday data and handles important tasks, staying with the original software may be the smarter choice.

**The real question is not whether you can root your Android device. It is whether you actually need to.**
